final.mechanism: A process inside carts began consuming CPU (2.76 -> 67.39, 24x) and memory (203 -> 1311 MiB) simultaneously, without any increase in request traffic, saturating the container and slowing its request handling. This first degraded carts' own latency (5.75x), which then cascaded to front-end (1.65x, the alert) and orders (4.28x) as they waited on carts.

A resource problem inside catalogue caused its CPU usage to spike ~406x and memory ~60x starting 3s after the alert, despite request rate staying flat (1.04x). This internal failure ballooned catalogue's latency 48x, which propagated downstream and drove front-end's request latency from 0.0529 to 0.101 (1.90x).

The payment service's request latency spiked ~40x (0.005s to 0.207s) starting 13s after the alert, with no increase in error rate, memory, disk I/O, or open sockets, and only a modest workload rise (1.07x) that stayed in normal range. This indicates a process-level performance degradation in payment itself, which slowed payment-dependent requests and degraded front-end latency.

The user service's request handling stalled internally: its latency rose 68x (9ms to 601ms) while its CPU dropped to 0.22x with no memory, socket, or backend saturation — an idle-but-hung process rather than a resource- or dependency-bound one. Every front-end and orders request that called user then blocked on it, producing front-end's 1.55x mean latency, orders' 20x latency, and eventually front-end timeout errors.

The carts process stalled: its CPU usage collapsed to 0.37x while its request latency exploded 63x and incoming traffic backed off to 0.58x, indicating carts stopped doing work rather than being overloaded. The latency propagated to orders (17.7x) and the user-facing front-end (10.75x), and carts-db's later disk I/O rise (starting 201s after the alert) is a downstream backlog effect, not the cause.

A runaway process or resource leak inside payment caused CPU usage to spike ~115x and memory ~57x starting ~11s after the alert, with no increase in request rate. This degraded payment's own request latency ~15x, which propagated up to the front-end, producing the user-facing latency alert.

The carts service developed an internal resource/process problem (CPU-bound slowdown): its CPU usage spiked ~13x with no increase in request load or memory, degrading its own latency 1.39x, which cascaded into the front-end's 1.56x latency increase.

A runaway process or memory leak inside the user service caused CPU usage to spike ~32x and memory to grow ~60x within 4 seconds of the alert, saturating the service. This slowed user's request handling (latency up 9.36x), which cascaded to front-end (2.04x) and orders (2.94x) as they wait on user, with no traffic increase to explain the load.

The user service's request latency jumped ~150x (0.00565 -> 0.84) starting 20s after the alert, with no change in its incoming request rate and no resource saturation anywhere (user CPU up only 1.28x and user-db CPU/disk/memory all within normal range). This points to a process-level problem inside user itself (e.g., stalled handler or connection handling), whose slow responses backed up open sockets (left normal range at +27s) and propagated the delay to front-end, raising its latency 1.05x.

A runaway process inside payment began consuming CPU (446x) and memory (100x) simultaneously at +10s with no increase in request rate, exhausting its resources and slowing its request handling 31x. That latency cascaded up the synchronous call chain — orders (5.26x at +33s) waiting on payment, then front-end (1.07x at +284s) waiting on orders — producing the user-facing latency alert.

A process problem inside orders caused its CPU usage to spike ~47x (0.93 to 43.77) while request volume stayed flat, saturating the service and slowing order processing 1.86x with no errors or memory growth. The added order-processing delay propagated up to front-end (and secondarily to user, carts, queue-master, shipping), producing the user-facing latency alert.

The carts process began burning ~31x its normal CPU at +9s despite flat request volume and flat memory, saturating the service. This inflated carts' own request latency (3.45x at +14s), which propagated downstream to orders (1.92x) and the user-facing front-end (1.60x), triggering the alert.

A resource/process fault inside the user service caused its CPU usage to spike ~27x with no change in request volume, saturating the service and inflating its request latency ~34x, which propagated to the front-end's latency alert.

A runaway process (CPU leak/hot loop) in catalogue drove CPU from 0.17 to 18.33 cores at alert time, degrading its request processing. This propagated to dependent services (front-end, carts) as slightly elevated latency.

A process problem in carts caused its CPU usage to spike ~44x and memory to triple starting ~10s after the alert, with no increase in request traffic. Carts became CPU/memory-bound, its own latency rose 1.57x, and this propagated to the front-end, raising user-facing latency 1.23x.

The user service suffered a runaway resource problem: beginning 3s after the alert, its CPU usage exploded 23.4x and its memory usage grew 108x (6 MiB to ~670-800 MiB) with no increase in incoming traffic (0.99x) and no errors, indicating a fault in the user process itself (e.g., a memory leak or runaway allocation loop). This resource saturation drove user's request latency up 10.1x, which degraded the user-facing front-end latency and triggered the alert.

A resource/process problem in orders itself (its CPU was already near saturation at ~0.96 cores before the alert and then climbed to a 2.23-core max) caused severe request queueing: orders latency spiked 44x within 14s of the alert, and as front-end calls to orders stalled and timed out, front-end latency rose 1.23x and both services began erroring at +44s, while stuck orders stopped issuing downstream calls (payment and shipping traffic dropped to 0.57x).

A process/resource problem inside catalogue caused its CPU usage to spike ~263x (with memory and open sockets also rising) starting 3s after the alert, with no increase in incoming traffic. The resulting CPU saturation slowed catalogue's request handling (latency 6x), which propagated to the front-end and raised user-facing latency.

A resource/process problem in payment (massive CPU saturation ~117x, plus memory and open-socket growth starting 19s after the alert) caused its latency to spike 30x, which stalled order completion and slowed the front-end's user-facing requests.

Catalogue's process stalled internally at +9s (CPU usage fell to 0.57x) and its connections to catalogue-db dropped from 4 to 2.8, so it stopped servicing queries: its own latency exploded 344x at +17s, requests and sockets piled up (6 to 10-19, memory 6 to 9-11 MiB), and front-end degraded 2.26x at +21s as a downstream consequence.

A resource/process problem inside the user service caused its CPU usage to spike ~17.5x (mean 1.00 -> 17.51) and memory to grow 1.64x within seconds of the alert, despite request rate staying flat. This made user requests 9.23x slower, which propagated up the call chain, degrading orders (3.71x) and front-end (1.72x) latency with no errors raised.

An internal resource/process problem in orders caused its CPU to spike ~55x and memory to climb to 1024 MiB starting 6s after the alert, with no increase in incoming traffic (0.99x). The degraded orders service slowed request handling (6.2x latency), which propagated to the front-end that calls it, driving the front-end's 1.61x latency alert.

An internal process/resource problem in payment caused its CPU (111.73x) and memory (2.19x) to spike 12s after the alert with no change in incoming request rate. The resulting saturation drove payment's request latency up 10.34x, which propagated to its caller orders (1.93x) and then to the user-facing front-end (1.02x), triggering the latency alert.

A problem inside catalogue (CPU-bound process/resource issue) made its request latency spike ~228x starting +10s after the alert, with no errors returned. Slow responses caused open sockets to pile up (1.47x) and CPU to climb (1.27x) in catalogue, and the delay propagated to the front-end (1.35x latency). catalogue-db's mild CPU rise lagged (+46s) and its memory/disk stayed flat, consistent with it being a downstream consequence rather than the cause.

A disk I/O problem in carts-db (disk I/O rose 1.75x, leaving normal range) made database queries slow to complete. Backed-up queries caused connection/socket buildup (8 -> 13.55) and huge latency in carts (87x) and its caller orders (19x), which propagated to the front-end (22.56x).

A process-level fault inside the catalogue service (runaway CPU burn, ~271x, with memory nearly doubling and open sockets tripling, all departing ~+20s after the alert) slowed its request handling 16.66x with no errors and no traffic change, degrading the user-facing path through front-end. The database was not involved — every catalogue-db resource metric stayed flat.

A resource problem inside ts-order-service (memory/CPU ballooning) caused its request latency to rise 8.26x starting ~19s after the alert, which propagated to dependent services and drove up user-facing latency in ts-ui-dashboard.

A process/resource problem inside ts-order-service drove CPU from 3.65 to 35.66 (nearly 10x) starting ~15s after the alert, with request traffic unchanged. This CPU saturation slowed the service's request handling (latency 3.51x, from 0.0241 to 0.0845), which propagated up the call chain to degrade ts-ui-dashboard's user-facing latency.

ts-train-service suffered an internal process/resource problem: its CPU usage jumped ~7.8x (mean 4.46 to 34.89) while its incoming request rate stayed flat (0.92x), so the CPU burn was not load-driven. The resulting saturation inflated its own request latency ~55x, and every downstream service that performs train lookups (travel, travel2, seat, preserve, ticketinfo, consign, basic) inherited the delay, surfacing as the 3.07x latency increase on ts-ui-dashboard.

Excessive disk I/O inside ts-auth-service (first anomaly, +4s) caused request processing to slow (latency 3.38x, CPU 2.5x), and since every dashboard request passes through authentication, this cascaded into the 3.02x latency spike on ts-ui-dashboard.

The orders process developed an internal fault (a CPU-bound spin loop): with incoming request rate flat (1.92 -> 1.85), its CPU exploded 14.65x (2.84 -> 41.66) within 8 seconds of the alert, and its open sockets grew 1.74x at the same onset, while memory, disk, and error rates stayed flat. CPU saturation made orders' own latency rise 1.85x (0.997 -> 1.84s), and since front-end and carts call orders, that queuing delay propagated as the 1.24x front-end latency increase that triggered the alert.

A runaway process or disk-level fault in ts-route-service caused an extreme disk I/O explosion (~230,000x) starting 5s after the alert, saturating CPU (2.87x), memory (1.88x), and socket connections. This resource saturation caused ts-route-service request latency to spike 4.69x, cascading latency to downstream services (admin-travel, preserve, travel, order, and ultimately ts-ui-dashboard).

A process/resource problem inside ts-auth-service drove CPU usage up 4.4x starting just 4s after the alert, with no increase in incoming request rate. The CPU saturation slowed the service (latency 2.14x), causing connection/queue buildup (sockets +20%) which propagated latency to ts-ui-dashboard and downstream services like ts-order-service.

A resource/process problem inside ts-travel-service caused its CPU usage to spike ~40x while latency rose 6.86x. The service slowed down rather than failed (error rate stayed at 0), so requests queued and completed slowly, which propagated the latency up to the user-facing ts-ui-dashboard.

An internal CPU-bound fault (e.g., a hot loop, spin, or pathological processing path) in ts-travel-service drove its CPU to 5.33x baseline at unchanged request rate, doubling its latency. All travel-dependent services (ts-seat-service, ts-food-service, ts-preserve-service, ts-admin-travel-service, and the user-facing ts-ui-dashboard) inherited the slowdown while blocking on travel, which propagated the latency alert on ts-ui-dashboard.

A network/process-level fault in ts-auth-mongo caused it to stop serving requests promptly despite idle resources: connections began queuing at mongo first (+8s), then ts-auth-service stalled (latency 0.262 -> 0.906, 3.46x at +16s) waiting on auth queries, propagating the slowdown to ts-ui-dashboard (+26s). Flat CPU, disk, and memory on mongo alongside its flat resource use rule out saturation at auth, indicating a stall (e.g., network or process issue) inside ts-auth-mongo itself.

Something in ts-travel-service's request path stalled: its latency rose 3.47x (+45s) while CPU, memory, disk, and incoming traffic (0.90x) all stayed flat, so requests hung in wait rather than being compute-, resource-, or load-bound. Callers' connections piled up (sockets +22% at +44s) and the delay cascaded to admin-travel, preserve, food, seat, and finally ts-ui-dashboard, whose latency rose 1.33x.

A runaway resource problem in ts-travel-service began ~20s after the alert: disk I/O exploded 442x, CPU rose 12.8x (2.74 -> 34.89 cores), and memory ballooned from 273 MiB to a 1024 MiB max, saturating the service. With no traffic increase (1.05x), this internal process/disk problem slowed ts-travel-service's request handling (latency 0.12 -> 0.711, 5.9x), which propagated through its dependents (ts-seat-service, ts-preserve-service, ts-food-service, ts-admin-travel-service) to ts-ui-dashboard, nearly doubling user-facing latency.

ts-route-service's process began burning CPU internally (CPU 4.43→34.98, a 7.90x jump) despite falling request volume (0.79x), saturating its CPU and inflating its request latency 9.49x. This stalled its upstream callers (admin-travel, travel, ticketinfo, food, and the ts-ui-dashboard frontend), producing the user-facing latency alert.

A process-level disk I/O fault inside ts-order-service began at +11s, driving disk I/O from ~50k to ~305k (6.02x, peaks at 2.1M — 22x its prior max). With traffic, CPU, sockets, and memory all flat, order's request threads blocked in I/O wait, raising its latency 6.78x; its callers (inside-payment, preserve, security, seat) then degraded and the delay propagated to ts-ui-dashboard (1.21x).

ts-order-service suffered a resource/process failure beginning ~5s after the alert: CPU spiked 5.67x (5.36 -> 30.34), memory grew 1.82x (264 -> 480 MiB), and open sockets rose 1.31x, all while its request rate stayed flat (0.95x). This saturation drove its own latency up 1.77x (0.0987 -> 0.175) with no errors, and that slowdown propagated up the call chain to ts-ui-dashboard, producing the 1.13x user-facing latency alert.

A resource/process problem inside ts-train-service (CPU saturation to ~11x baseline, with parallel disk I/O and open-socket growth, at unchanged request volume) made the service extremely slow, raising its own latency ~9.3x and propagating to upstream services including the user-facing ts-ui-dashboard (1.72x).

A memory leak/pressure in ts-travel-service caused its memory to balloon (266→478 MiB) and triggered massive disk I/O (~12 GB/s, 227,682x) plus CPU burn (4.22x) on essentially unchanged traffic (1.12x), starting at +13s. This slowed travel-service itself (2.20x latency) and caused all callers — ts-ui-dashboard, ts-food-service, ts-admin-travel-service, ts-seat-service, ts-preserve-service, ts-auth-service — to queue behind it, producing the user-facing latency alert.

A resource problem in ts-auth-service (CPU up 2.24x, memory up 2.02x, sockets up 1.42x, all starting ~13s after the alert time) slowed its request handling (latency 2.46x) despite unchanged traffic, which propagated to ts-ui-dashboard's 2.22x latency increase. With zero errors, the service degraded but did not fail outright.

An internal process/connection-handling problem in ts-train-service caused its request latency to balloon ~18.8x despite flat incoming traffic and healthy disk, memory, and CPU — requests queued or blocked inside the service. The slowdown propagated up through its callers (ts-seat-service, ts-travel-service, ts-preserve-service, ts-admin-travel-service) to ts-ui-dashboard, producing the user-facing latency alert.

A network/connection-level fault inside ts-route-service made its requests hang: latency rose 51x with zero errors and no CPU, memory, or disk saturation, while open sockets piled up 1.55x from +17s as connections stalled. Every service that depends on route queries then queued behind it, cascading the 7.66x latency increase into ts-ui-dashboard.

ts-train-service's process began burning CPU (~3 -> ~33, 10.86x) at flat request volume, degrading its own latency 7.17x; the slowdown then propagated to its callers (ts-admin-travel-service, ts-ticketinfo-service, ts-basic-service, ts-seat-service), which showed latency spikes with no resource anomalies of their own.

ts-order-service suffered a severe internal resource failure: CPU spiked 10x (3.5 to 35) with disk I/O up 3.4x and open sockets more than doubling, all starting ~9s after the alert, while its incoming request rate stayed nearly flat (1.11x). This saturation slowed its own request handling (latency 6x), and the delay propagated through dependent services (ts-preserve, ts-security, ts-inside-payment, ts-seat) to the user-facing ts-ui-dashboard, whose latency rose 1.65x.

A CPU-bound runaway inside the ts-route-service process (CPU 5.09→35.59 cores, 7x, with flat request traffic, flat memory, zero errors, and a flat ts-route-mongo) made every route query ~10x slower (0.009→0.091s). This added latency propagated up through every service that calls route (admin-travel, basic, food, ticketinfo, travel, preserve) and produced the 1.82x latency alert on ts-ui-dashboard.

A process problem in ts-auth-service caused its resource usage to spiral out of control: memory doubled (249->498 MiB), disk I/O exploded ~368x (55k->20.2M), and CPU rose 2.44x (14.8->36.1), all within 3 seconds of the alert, while its request rate stayed flat. This resource pathology (likely memory-driven disk thrashing) slowed its request handling (latency 0.609->2.09, 3.44x), which propagated through dependent services to inflate ts-ui-dashboard latency.

ts-route-service suffered a massive abnormal disk I/O surge (6.16x the before mean, peaking at 2.24M) starting ~11s after the alert, which stalled its request handling and inflated its own latency 12.76x; this bottleneck propagated to dependent services (seat, travel, food, admin-travel, ui-dashboard), producing the user-facing latency alert. CPU was flat and traffic actually fell, ruling out a load-driven cause.

A process/memory problem in ts-route-service caused its CPU usage to explode (3.85 -> 42.69, 11.1x) and its memory to balloon (254 MiB -> 462 MiB, 1.82x), both starting at +5s. This made route-service extremely slow (latency 0.0075 -> 0.103, 13.7x, starting +15s), and since downstream services (travel, preserve, food, admin-travel, ticketinfo, etc.) call route-service, their latencies degraded in cascade, raising ts-ui-dashboard latency 3.4x.

Starting at +18s, orders entered a fault state: CPU spiked 27x (1.87 -> 51.02), memory nearly doubled (320 -> 608 MiB), its error rate went from zero to 6.42, and its request rate tripled. Front-end calls into the failing orders service produced the front-end error rate (0 -> 3.17) and the observed 1.14x latency increase; front-end's own workload did not increase (0.83x), ruling out a load-driven front-end problem.

Payment's process degraded at +17s (memory grew 1.47x and the process stalled, halving its CPU), so payment requests hung: latency rose 49.57x, open sockets piled up 5-to-9, and throughput fell to 0.40x. Orders' calls into payment then timed out, producing orders/front-end errors and the user-facing latency alert, while fewer completed orders starved shipping/queue-master.
